title: QGIS Handbook
text:
Introduction
A Geographic Information System (GIS) is a powerful way to work with information that’s tied to locations on Earth. This type of information, often called geospatial data, includes anything that has a geographic reference, such as coordinates, addresses, or map features. GIS allows you to store, view, analyse, and present these data so you can understand spatial patterns and relationships.
In this course, you will learn how to use GIS to solve a real-world problem: deciding where to build a wind farm. Through a series of practical exercises, you will bring together many different datasets, including land use, protected areas, topography, and average wind speed, to identify the most suitable location for a new wind farm in part of the Welsh landscape.
By the end of the course, you will be able to:

Load, explore, and manage different types of geospatial data.
Create maps and visualisations using QGIS.
Analyse spatial data to assess suitability for development.
Apply common planning and environmental constraints to real-world scenarios.

The skills you gain here can also be applied to a wide range of other questions, from identifying flood risk zones to planning urban transport routes or mapping wildlife habitats — anywhere location matters.

title: Before you begin
text:
Accessing QGIS
This chapter will help you build practical skills, avoid common pitfalls, and make the most of your time in the computer lab. You can work at your own pace, but it is important to attend all scheduled computer practicals. These sessions are your chance to share your progress, ask questions, and clear up misunderstandings in a supportive, flipped-learning environment (Dikilitas and Fructuoso 2023). By the end of this chapter, you’ll be better prepared to complete the exercises efficiently and confidently.
There are a number of ways to access QGIS:

text:
University computerPersonal computerRemote Desktop


QGIS can be accessed from any computer around campus:

Use the ZenWorks window to navigate to Science → Geography
Double-click the QGIS icon



QGIS is free, open-source software available for Windows, Mac, and Linux. This means you’re not limited to using University computers. You can install it on your own machine and work wherever and whenever you like:

Download and install QGIS here
Double-click on the downloaded folder to start the installation. For Mac users, right-click on the folder and click Open to start the installation







Tip



I recommend installing the Long Term Release version of QGIS which, in theory, has fewer bugs in it. Download Latest Release for the most up-to-date features.




The Remote Desktop allows you to log into one of the University’s Open Access computers from home. Once connected, you will have the same access to software and data as if you were physically on campus — including the Student Common L:drive (L:/College of Science/Geography/GEG276).






Note



The number of simultaneous Remote Desktop connections is capped, so you may not always be able to log in.


Using the Remote Desktop requires:

The Microsoft Authenticator app installed on a smartphone.
VPN access (see the University IT guidance).

Download the Microsoft Authenticator App from your app store.
Go to the MyUni hub. and log in.

Select Secure my Account (bottom right).

If the setup doesn’t work the first time, repeat the steps carefully to confirm each stage is complete. If you are still experiencing issues, please follow the online tutorials at Remote PC Access Service and Account Enquiry and MFA Setup, request support from the IT team using the Service Centre, or contact me for guidance.

title: Before you begin
text:
Accessing the data

Check this works: Go to OneDrive on the web (onedrive.live.com or your work/school portal). Navigate to Shared in the left sidebar, then find the folder shared with you Open the folder and click Sync in the top toolbar. This will download and sync the folder to your PC, and it’ll appear in File Explorer under your OneDrive section

title: Before you begin
text:
Data storage
Swansea University provides secure storage through OneDrive and network drives. These appear the same no matter which University computer you log into, and you can also access OneDrive from your own devices. I have two key tips for you:

Always save your work to OneDrive. This keeps it safe from accidental loss and accessible wherever you are. Avoid storing coursework on the local C: drive. Files saved there are only available on that one machine and may be deleted automatically overnight.
Be organised. Create a clear folder structure for your GIS work and name files logically. GIS projects can generate hundreds of files. Staying tidy will save you time and frustration later.

title: Before you begin
text:
Watch your storage space
If your disk space becomes full, QGIS and other software can crash. To remedy this:

Check available space by right-clicking your OneDrive network in Windows Explorer and clicking Properties
Delete temporary or unwanted files to free up space

If problems persist (e.g. you can’t log in, access software, or save files), make a Service Centre request here.

title: Before you begin
text:
GIS software options
Two software applications presently dominate the GIS market, each with benefits and drawbacks:

ESRI ArcGIS Pro. ArcGIS Pro has been the industry leader for decades and is widely used by professionals.


Pros: Well established, feature-rich, and supported by extensive online documentation. Cons: Software is licensed and expensive.


QGIS (Quantum GIS). QGIS is an open-source application that has grown rapidly in popularity, especially in the public sector.


Pros: Free to install, open source, and increasingly competitive with ArcGIS. Cons: Still lacks some advanced functions and may be less common in certain job markets.

As a Geography Department, we’ve chosen to teach you QGIS. Why? Because it combines the power and flexibility of professional GIS with the accessibility and freedom of open-source software.
QGIS is free to install on your own computer, meaning you can practise and experiment anywhere, anytime, without relying on campus labs or expensive licences. It has a clean, intuitive interface that many beginners find easier to learn than ArcGIS, yet it still offers advanced tools used by professionals around the world.
Beyond the classroom, QGIS is rapidly gaining ground in government, consultancy, and research sectors, particularly where budgets are tight and data-sharing is important (Graser et al. 2025). Its open-source nature means new features and plugins are added by a global community of GIS experts. You’re therefore learning with a platform that’s evolving at the cutting edge.
Mastering QGIS now gives you a career-ready skillset, the ability to collaborate internationally without licence barriers, and the confidence that you can always access a powerful GIS toolkit long after graduation.

title: Before you begin
text:
Developing your computer skills
The most effective way to learn GIS is to use it. The practical exercises are designed to guide you through the most common functions in QGIS, helping you build skills and create results you can use in your coursework, projects, or dissertation.
Here are my protips for learning QGIS:

Expect to make mistakes and repeat steps. This repetition will help you remember processes. QGIS can occasionally hang or crash. Learn to recover quickly by saving often and keeping track of your progress.
Save your work regularly and know exactly where it is stored. Keep a tidy, logical folder structure, and make copies of work that has taken a long time to achieve. GIS creates many files, and good organisation will save time and prevent data loss.
Explore the software rather than only following instructions. Be bold and click through menus, try tools, and experiment. You will learn faster by discovering features yourself. The practical exercises will expect you to find some things out for yourself.
Ask for help when needed. Support is available through Canvas video demos, classmates, demonstrators, and online resources. Coursework must be completed individually, but collaboration on problem-solving is encouraged.

title: Before you begin
text:
QGIS basics

Windows, panels, and toolbars
QGIS has two main windows: the Map Canvas and Print Layout. Within each window, you can open a number of toolbars (located along the top or left of each window by default) and panels (such as the Attribute Table to view and edit data linked to map features). You need to become familiar with opening and interacting with these main program elements.



The Map Canvas (top) and Print Layout (bottom) windows, with toolbars along the top (both windows) and left (Print Layout window only) of each window, and a series of panels which are either docked or floating (e.g. an Attributes Table (right)).




Layers
A layer is a dataset of a single type — vector or raster — loaded into QGIS from (often multiple associated) files saved on your network. Layers are combined to create maps or are processed to produce new layers. Layer order matters because higher layers can hide lower ones.


Projects
A QGIS project file (.qgz) stores references to your data and display settings, but doesn’t store the data itself. Projects therefore contain virtual links to all of the data files you’ve loaded, as well as instructions to the software as to how they should be displayed. This leads to three important considerations:

Moving QGIS projects. Copying or transferring a QGIS project from one computer to another would require copying the project file and all associated data layers in such a way as to maintain the relative file paths (the path to your data the QGIS project needs to load them). This is sometimes difficult to achieve. If you change your computer environment (e.g. from the University system to your laptop), it is often easier simply to copy all of the layer files and start a new project from scratch.
Moving or renaming data layers. Changing data layers (or the folders that contain them) will mean a QGIS project can no longer find them and so will fail to open them. It is possible to recover from this situation, but it’s easier to avoid in the first place. All data files on the master OneDrive will remain where they are. Make sure that all data files that you put on your OneDrive (or memory stick or laptop disk) are named sensibly and placed in an appropriate folder structure so that you don’t accidentally move, rename, or delete them. You will probably generate many hundreds of data files by downloading (e.g. from the internet), copying (e.g. from OneDrive), or creating layers in the course of GIS processing.
Working with temporary layers. When you create a new GIS layer (e.g. by performing a geoprocessing function on an existing layer), you are normally presented with the option of creating a temporary layer or saving the new layer to disk. Creating temporary layers is a quick way of exploring and confirming the output is what you wanted. However, these layers will no longer be available when you close the project unless you make them permanent. I recommend that use temporary layers for experimentation, and choose a permanent name, location, and data type for any layer that you will need later on.



Plugins
The basic installation of QGIS is adequate for most purposes, however the GIS practical exercises here go a bit beyond this basic functionality. Many QGIS add-ons have been developed through open source software development and made freely available through the Plugins interface. Plugins are installed in the user part of the computer storage so require no administrator privileges. You are encouraged to explore all available plugins. The practical exercises will explain when certain plugins need to be installed.

title: Before you begin
text:
Key considerations

Printing maps
Printed colours often look different from the colours you see on screen. If you need to print a map, always check that your chosen colours work well on paper. The best way to check this is to print a test copy, inspect it closely to make sure all map elements are clear and distinguishable, and adjust the colours if necessary. You may need to repeat this process a few times to get the result you want. Fortunately, all GEG276 coursework (and most assignments in other modules) is submitted online, so printing is rarely essential. Printers also usually cannot print right to the edges of the paper. If you plan to print directly from QGIS, leave at least a 0.5 cm margin around your map to avoid cutting off important details.


Using transparency
Transparency can help combine multiple layers without losing important details, but it can also make map colours inconsistent with the legend. Avoid partial transparency in final maps for coursework unless it adds essential meaning. Colours in the legend should match those in the map exactly.


GIS file types
There are several GIS file types. For raster data, I recommend saving them as GeoTIFF (.tif). For vector data (points, lines, or polygons), I recommend saving them as GeoPackage (.gpkg). You will likely come across Shapefiles as a format for storing vector data. This format has been around since the 90s and remains in wide use today. I recommend using GeoPackages instead for two reasons:

Efficient storage. A shapefile stores data as a number of files (between 3 and 16!) which have the same name but different extensions (.shp, .shx, .dbf…). If you rename or share a shapefile, you need to make sure that you rename all files and share all files for the new version to work correctly.
Flexible storage. A shapefile can only be a point, line, or polygon per file. A GeoPackage can store multiple data types.



GIS data sources
Use reputable sources for GIS data. In the UK, Ordnance Survey (OS) provides authoritative datasets, some of which are free via OS OpenData. As a Swansea University student, you can also access premium OS data through EDINA Digimap. Open data projects like OpenStreetMap offer free, continuously updated alternatives that are widely used in research and community projects. These data are continuously improving in quality and coverage and anyone can get involved in the project. I’ve chosen to use only Open Data sources for the practical exercises and project so that there are no restrictions on sharing data.


Customising the Map Canvas (advanced)
If you’re like me and you like a nice minimalist and clear interface to work with, one can customise the QGIS Map Canvas to a high degree. If you wish to do this, I recommend you explore the QGIS Documentation at your leisure here. But be careful! You may end up removing particular tools or menus that are essential for the completion of this course. So I recommend you only experiment with customisation after you’ve completed the course.

title: Before you begin
text:
Getting help
For general information, please refer to the GEG276 Canvas site. All documents associated with the course will be posted there, and I may use the Canvas Discussion Board to share extra information. If you don’t find what you’re looking for, feel free to email me. If I receive a query (the answer to which may be useful to all students), I will post a reply via email or the Discussion Board.
Software-specific problems can often be solved by Googling and asking AI. Typing QGIS and a description of your problem can often lead to a solution. Community-led sites like StackExchange are especially useful for getting help. The QGIS manual, QGIS Forum, and the main QGIS website are all valuable sources too.




Dikilitas, K., and I. N. Fructuoso. 2023. “Conceptual Framework for Flexible Learning Design: The Context of Flipped Classroom.” Learning Design for Flexible Education, nos. 2022-1-ES01-KA220-HED-000085250: 1–46. https://kudos.dfo.no/documents/77155/files/37244.pdf.


Graser, Anita, Tim Sutton, and Marco Bernasocchi. 2025. “The QGIS Project: Spatial Without Compromise.” Patterns 6 (7): 101265. https://doi.org/https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patter.2025.101265.

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.1 Starting up
To master QGIS, one must start with the basics. This exercise introduces the foundational skills that will underpin the development of your wind farm project and beyond - including your dissertation. Take your time, ask questions, and make sure you are confident with each step before moving on.

title: 1  Getting started
text:
Follow the steps here to access all the datasets you need for the practicals and the final project
Launch QGIS. This could be on a University computer, via a remote desktop, or on your own computer
From the menu bar, click Project → New. Find the shortcut icon to create a new project
Add your first vector layer in QGIS:

From the menu bar, click Layer → Add Layer → Add Vector Layer...
Click the Browse icon ()
Navigate to the folder where the data is stored, i.e. GEG276
Open the British_Isles_land_polygons folder and click on the corresponding .gpkg vector layer
Click Open → Add → Close. This dataset from the OpenStreetMap project consists of polygons representing the many islands making up the British Isles. Note the layer is now listed under the Layers panel. You can also drag-and-drop datasets from the browser straight into the Map Canvas

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.2 Navigation

Use the Map Navigation Toolbar to explore this dataset by panning and zooming







Try using the mouse scroll wheel as a shortcut
Make yourself familiar with navigating around the Map Canvas by losing yourself! Pan and zoom until you can’t see the British Isles layer anymore. Once lost, right-click on the layer in the Layers panel and click Zoom to Layer(s) to easily return to view that layer

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.3 Adjusting style properties

To adjust a layer’s symbology:

From the Layers panel, right-click on British_Isles_land_polygons and click Properties... → Symbology. A useful shortcut to Properties is to double-click the layer
Click Simple Fill and experiment with changing the layer symbology’s colours, styles, and widths. You have complete control over how vector layers appear. When designing a map, consider carefully how to choose an appropriate style for each layer
Click Apply → OK when you’ve finished editing the layer’s symbology








From the menu bar, click Project → Save and save your project to a suitable location. Find the shortcut. Remember to save regularly from now on!

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.4 Measuring geospatial objects

Click the drop-down arrow next to the Measure icon to select the appropriate tool for measuring:

The distance between the extreme cardinal points of Great Britain (in miles)
The approximate area of the Isle of Man (in square kilometres)








Use left-click to add points, and right-click to stop taking the length / area measurements



What is the distance between the extreme cardinal points of Great Britain (in miles)?



The distance between the extreme cardinal points of Great Britain was 603 miles.




What is the approximate area of the Isle of Man (in square kilometres)?



The approximate area of the Isle of Man was 571 square kilometres.

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.5 Exploring the Attribute Table

From the Layers panel, right-click on British_Isles_land_polygons and click Open Attribute Table. An attribute table is a fundamental part of all GIS datasets. Each row of the table corresponds to a single feature (e.g. a polygon) of the vector layer, and each column, or attribute (of which there can be as many as is needed), records a property of the feature (e.g. name, area, circumference). This particular data layer has two attributes: fid (field identifier) and Area
Click the Dock Attribute Table icon () so that you can see both the Map Canvas and Attribute Table on screen at once
To understand how the attribute table corresponds with the vector layer:

Sort the attribute table according to each polygon’s area by clicking the Area column title. Repeated clicks will sort by ascending or descending the values
Click a row number to select the polygon to which it corresponds. The selected polygon in the Map Canvas has now been highlighted yellow
Click the Zoom map to the selected rows icon in the top-right corner () to zoom to the selected polygon in the Map Canvas








Repeat the step above to explore the ten largest islands of the British Isles



Can you name the seventh-largest island of the British Isles?

SkyeLewis and HarrisIslayYnys Môn / AngleseyYnys Enlli / Bardsey



The seventh-largest island of the British Isles is Ynys Môn / Anglesey.



You can also select features in the Map Canvas to identify their corresponding attributes in the attributes table:

Click the Select Features icon ()
Select (highlight in yellow) the Isle of Wight
In the attribute table, click the Move selection to top icon () to move the selected line of the table to the top
Read the area of the feature - which is in square metres - and convert it to square km (i.e. divide by 1,000,000)




What is the precise area of the Isle of Wight (in square kilometres)?



The precise area of the Isle of Wight was 382 square kilometres.



Click the Deselect features icon () to deselect the current selection. These functions will be very useful later on

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.6 Arranging layers

Add the Wales_Principal_Areas.gpkg layer in the UK_Boundaries folder to your project. This dataset consists of polygons representing the Principal Areas (otherwise known as counties) of Wales. Note this layer will also appear in the Layers panel
Adjust the style of this layer and explore its attribute table
Experiment with switching layer visibility on or off using the tick boxes in the Layers panel (). This becomes essential when managing multiple layers in a project
Change the order of the layers by dragging each upwards or downwards in the layer panel
Move Wales_Principle_Areas to the top of the Layers panel. Notice how the seaward political (Principal Area) boundary of Wales goes beyond the coastline (Land Polygons). This is because the physical land boundary is generally classified according to the mean high water mark, while administrative boundaries are normally classified according to the mean low water mark. That’s Geography!
To categorise the layer’s symbology:

Open the layer’s Symbology window
Use the drop-down menu to change the symbology source from Single Symbol to Categorized
Use the Value drop-down menu to select the attribute name
Click Classify → OK. How colourful!

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.7 Labelling layers

To label layers:

Select Wales_Principal_Areas layer in the Layers panel
From the menu bar, click Layer → Labeling. Find the shortcut to this window (hint - check out Properties...)
Use the drop-down menu to change the labelling source from No Labels to Single Labels
Change the Value drop-down menu to label the Wales Principle Area polygons according to their English or Welsh names

Experiment with modifying the labels by:

Changing the text style () e.g. style and size
Changing the label format () e.g. wrapping and orientation
Adding a text buffer ()
Changing the label placement ()
Playing around with other options. You are in complete control!
Have you saved your project recently?

Now that the Principal Areas have been labelled, zoom out. Notice how QGIS chooses to place and resize the labels so that they remain visible, but switches some of them off to avoid overlapping text. This is a fundamental part of map design and QGIS tries to optimize readability. You can control this behavior through the Labeling window and you are encouraged to experiment.

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.8 Adding and filtering data

Add the vector layer Wales_operational_windfarms.gpkg to your project. These data are from the UK Renewable Energy Planning Database and represent the location of operational wind farms across Wales
Examine the attribute table
Adjust the layer’s style, noting that point data is represented in a different way to polygon data
Label the wind farms by their name or by their generation capacity
Add the vector layer gis_osm_roads_free_1.gpkg, which is in the folder British_Isles_geofabrik → wales, to your project. These data form part of the OpenStreetMap project and represent all roads in Wales. This is a large dataset and may take time to load and display
Once again, for this layer:

Examine the attribute table
Experiment with different styles for line data

There is a lot of data here! So let’s subset it. There are many ways to make subsets of data layers to select only the data you need or that you want to display. To filter the data universally:

Right-click on the roads layer and click Filter...
This tool allows you to easily see all the unique values contained in each field (or column) of the attribute table. Click fclass → All. You can now see all the unique classes of road in the vector layer
Under Provider Specific Filter Expression, type "fclass" IN ('primary', 'trunk', 'motorway'). Make sure of precise punctuation and spacing
Click OK. Your map should now only display roads classed as primary and secondary. A funnel icon () has also appeared next to the layer in name in the `Layers’ panel, to remind you a filter has been applied

Label the roads with the attribute ref (i.e. the road number). See how these labels are displayed as you zoom in and out of the map
To remove the filter:

Click the funnel icon () next to the roads layer
CLick Clear → OK

To filter the data by defining what is presented in the map:

Open the layer’s Symbology window
Use the Categorized option to categorise the road symbology according to the fclass attribute
Delete all the road classes except primary, trunk, and motorway using the Delete icon (). See if you can make this task easier for yourself by using the Shift and Ctrl keys…
Double-click the line symbol per category to choose a suitable symbology for these remaining roads (e.g. thick red for primary, very thick light blue for motorway)

Add the gis_osm_waterways_free_1.gpkg vector layer in the British_Isles_geofabrik → wales folders. What colour would be best for this layer?

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.9 Adding external data

Navigate to datamap.gov.wales
Search for “Wales Coast Path” and click on the link
Under Select spatial data format, choose OGC Geopackage and click Download
Move the downloaded file to your OneDrive
Add the layer to your project and explore it
Try searching for and downloading other GIS data files from datamap.gov.wales, geofabrik.de, or any another source. Searching for geospatial datasets should show you how easy it can be to find and download data from the internet. This will also provide inspiration for dissertation ideas, which is now on your horizon

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.10 Have you finished?

Congratulations! You’ve learned the basics of QGIS. Make sure that you’ve understood all the steps above. Repeat if necessary, and ask for help or advice from the demonstrators. You will need this knowledge in future exercises and for the assessments.







NoteLearning outcomes



By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

Create and manage a QGIS project by adding vector layers from various sources and using the navigation tools to pan, zoom, and return to a layer’s extent
Adjust the appearance of spatial data through symbology, layer ordering, and labelling to build a clear, readable map
Explore the attribute table to understand how features relate to their attributes, sorting records and selecting features reciprocally between table and map canvas
Measure and filter geographic data by obtaining lengths and areas, converting between units, and subsetting layers using filter expressions and categorised symbology
Appreciate how cartographic and administrative conventions shape spatial representation, from automated label placement to the way boundaries are drawn

title: 2  Composing maps
text:
2.1 Creating a print layout
Communication of geographical data and concepts through maps is a fundamental skill for spatial scientists. Creating maps requires both the ability to make them complete, correct and functional, and the flair to make them interesting and attractive. This exercise introduces the QGIS Print Layout window, and is how you generate the maps for your wind farm project.

title: 2  Composing maps
text:
Launch QGIS and create a new project
Add the British_Isles_land_polygons.gpkg, Wales_border.gpkg, and Wales_Principal_Areas.gpkg layers to your project (the latter two are in the UK_Boundaries folder)
Label the Principal Areas of Wales in Welsh or English
To create a Print Layout:

Click Project → New Print Layout... (and find the shortcuts to this window)
Give the print layout an appropriate title
Click Project → Layout Manager.... You can see here the Print Layout now saved within your project. You can create more than one print layout per project. Use this panel to access and organise layouts
Click Close

Change the page orientation and size, so it fits onto an A4 portrait document with space beneath to fit a caption (see ?sec-WP):

Right‑click on the blank print layout
Click Page Properties...
Change Size to Custom
Reduce the map Height (e.g. to 270)
Change Orientation to Portrait

title: 2  Composing maps
section: 2.2 Adding and adjusting a map item
text:
2.2 Adding and adjusting a map item

Click Add Item → Add Map (look for the shortcut)
Draw a map onto the print layout. Map 1 should now appear under the Items tab







If necessary, adjust the map using the squares on the map boundaries so it fits more comfortably on the page
Select Map 1 from the Items panel
Set Scale to 1000000 (i.e. 1:1,000,000)
Use the Move item content () and Select/Move item () tools, and adjust the Scale value, to compose the map so that all of Wales is visible
Experiment with making fine adjustments to the scale by holding down the Ctrl key (windows) or Command key (mac) and scrolling the mouse wheel
Once you’re satisfied with the scaling, framing, and position, freeze the view in place by checking the box under the lock icon () for Map 1 in the Items panel
From the Map Canvas window, adjust layer styles:

Choose colours, border widths, and fonts that emphasise Wales and the difference between the outline of Wales (physical coast) and Principal Areas boundaries (non‑physical political construct)

Update the Print Layout to reflect your changes using one of these two options:

Click the Refresh icon () in the Print Layout window
Click the Update Map Preview icon () under Item Properties in the Map Canvas window

Click on the Item Properties tab and check Frame
Modify the frame’s Background colour appropriate for representing the ocean
You can modify the Layout and Item Properties of any item selected in the Item window. Note how the options under Layout and Item Properties tab update depending on what item you’ve selected. Remember that:

The order in which map items are listed is how they are also stacked on top of one another in the print layout
Some layer properties (e.g. layer order, style, labeling) are controlled in the Map Canvas

title: 2  Composing maps
section: 2.3 Adding a scale bar, north arrow, and grid
text:
2.3 Adding a scale bar, north arrow, and grid

From the Print Layout window, add a scale bar:

Click Add Item → Add Scale Bar
Drag and drop on the map to place it (you can move it later)
Select the scale bar from the Items panel
Click the Item Properties tab
Adjust the scale bar’s properties, notably Style, Scalebar units, Segments, Frame, and Background

Add a north arrow:

Click Add Item → Add North Arrow
Drag and drop on the map to place it (you can move it later)
Select the north arrow from the Items panel
Click the Item Properties tab
Under SVG Images, search arrow and choose a suitable north arrow
Adjust the north arrow’s properties, notably Fill color and Stroke color

Add a grid (aka graticule):

Select Map 1 from the Items panel
Click the Item Properties tab
Expand Grids
Click Add a new grid ()
Click Grid 1 → Modify Grid...
Set CRS to EPSG:4326 - WGS 84
Set X and Y intervals to 1 degrees
Check Draw Coordinates
Adjust the grid’s properties, notably Grid type, Frame, and Draw Coordinates. Can you adjust the labels for readability, soften the gridlines, and reduce unnecessary trailing zeros?

You may find that some of the map items, notably the coordinates, are now beyond the edge of the page. These will be lost when the map is exported! In these cases, you will need to adjust the map size periodically as you experiment with how to best arrange map items and the caption (see Section 2.2). Check how using Guides can aid you in aligning map items perfectly on the page.

title: 2  Composing maps
text:
2.4 Adding labels and a legend

Add a map title label:

Click Add Item → Add Label
Drag and drop on the map to place it (you can move it later)
Select the label from the Items panel
Click the Item Properties tab
Adjust the label’s properties, notably Main Properties, Font, Rotation, Frame, and Background

Add a legend:

Click Add Item → Add Legend
Drag and drop on the map to place it (you can move it later)
Select the legend from the Items panel
Click the Item Properties tab
Uncheck Auto update to enable modifications to the legend
Experiment with the legend toolbar icons () to improve the legend
Adjust the legend’s properties, notably Arrangement, Fonts and Text Formatting, Columns, Symbol, Spacing, Frame, and Background

title: 2  Composing maps
text:
2.5 Adding raster data

Add your first raster layer in QGIS:

From the menu bar in the Map Canvas, click Layer → Add Layer → Add Raster Layer...
Click the Browse icon () and navigate to the folder where the data is stored, i.e. GEG276
Open the Wales_mean_windspeed folder and click on any of the .tif raster layers
Click Open → Add → Close

Change the raster layer’s colour ramp:

Open the layer’s Properties... → Symbology
Use the Render type drop-down menu to select Singleband pseudocolor
Under Color ramp, select an appropriate colour ramp for the data (or pick one you just really like!)
Click OK

Adjust the order and modify the properties of the Wales Principal Areas and windspeed layers so both are visible at the same time. Hint: modifying Fill or Transparency properties may do nicely, but be careful to not break the link between the map and legend colours
In the Print Layout window, select Map 1 and click Update Map Preview under the Item Properties tab
If the colour scale for the raster layer does not appear in the legend, add it
Experiment with improving the aesthetics of the updated legend
Select Map 1 from the Items panel
Under Item Properties, check the Lock layers and Lock styles for layers to prevent further changes to the map. Uncheck if you need to make edits

title: 2  Composing maps
text:
2.6 Adding an inset map

Add a second map to provide an inset showing the British Isles (see Section 2.2)
Modify this second map to create an effective inset map that provides geographic context for the main map:

Adjust the inset map so the whole of the British Isles are visible
Modify which layers should be displayed by turning layer visibility on and off or changing the layer order
Modify the layers’ symbology








TipScale matters



Place emphasis on only a few, simply presented layers that are useful at this scale. Aim to be minimalist to avoid cluttering the map. Note that, because your map of Wales is locked, it’s not affected by changes in layer visibility or symbology being made for the inset. Herein lies the power of locking layers.



Add an extent indicator on your main map to connect it to the inset map:

Select your inset map (Map 2) from the Items panel
Under Item Properties, expand the Overviews tab
Click Add a new overview ()
Click Overview 1
Set the Map frame to your main map (Map 1)
Adjust the Frame style to draw a hollow rectangle with a thick line, to easily show the main map’s extent
Experiment further, especially with Fill color, Stroke color, and Join style

Projects can get rapidly out of control when multiple layers are used to build a map. It’s important to remove redundant layers and label items appropriately. E.g. try renaming Map 1 to Main, and Map 2 to Inset. This will help when you need to revisit and adjust your maps

title: 2  Composing maps
text:
2.7 Exporting your map

Ensure both maps have Lock layers checked so that your formatting is captured in the exported maps
To export your map as an image:

Click Layout → Export as Image...
Select a suitable location to save the map
Set the image format to PNG (.png)
Click Save
Set Export resolution to 300 dpi (300 dpi is suitable for viewing on a screen, 600 dpi is better for printing)
Click Save

Congratulations - you’ve created your first QGIS map assignment. Now make any revisions (including the map height) to be able to submit the best Map 1 that you can!







NoteLearning outcomes



By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

Create a scaled print layout in QGIS, setting page size and orientation and framing a map item at a fixed scale
Add the essential furniture of a complete map — scale bar, north arrow, graticule, title, caption, and legend — and adjust their properties for clarity
Integrate raster and vector data in a single layout, applying pseudocolour rendering and managing layer order and transparency so both remain legible
Construct an inset map using locked layers and an overview frame to place the main map in its wider geographic context
Export a print-ready map to PDF with appropriate vector, text, and compression settings, and appreciate how locking layers preserves scale integrity

title: 3  Geocoding and population
text:
3.1 Exploring postcode locations
The location and density of the human population underpin how society is organised. GIS helps one understand human systems, by calculating things like population density, proximity to features, and assigning data to addresses. In the UK, postcodes have been developed as a means to link human activity to physical locations for aiding governance. This exercise explores how postcodes can be used to gather useful population-level information, and how QGIS can be used to extract information - a valuable addition for your wind farm project.

title: 3  Geocoding and population
text:
Launch QGIS and create a new project
Add the Wales_Principal_Areas.gpkg layer to your project
Add the Wales_headcounts_at_postcodes_2021.gpkg layer to your project. This dataset contains the number of households and people registered at each postcode (taken from the 2021 Census), combined with coordinates from OS OpenData
Investigate the attribute table and explore how these points are distributed
Using attribute table selection and skills from Chapter 1 (Section 1.5), find postcodes with the greatest number of people in the Cardiff (CF), Swansea (SA) and Aberystwyth (SY) areas



How many people lived in the most populous postcode in the Cardiff (CF) area in 2021? (Enter the number without commas)



The most populous postcode in the Cardiff (CF) area in 2021 was 1,593.




How many people lived in the most populous postcode in the Swansea (SA) area in 2021? (Enter the number without commas)



The most populous postcode in the Swansea (SA) area in 2021 was 1,922.




How many people lived in the most populous postcode in the Aberystwyth (SY) area in 2021? (Enter the number without commas)



The most populous postcode in the Aberystwyth (SY) area in 2021 was 820.



Use Google Maps to search for these postcodes, and discuss with your neighbour why these locations have such high population counts



Match each postcode area to the feature in that postcode that had the highest registered population in 2021. (Enter the number without commas)



Cardiff (CF) = Prison
Swansea (SA) = Student halls
Aberystwyth (SY) = Student halls
Other Incorrect Match Options: • Hospital • Shopping centre • Council office



Save your project!
Open the headcounts layer’s Symbology window
Use the drop-down menu to change the symbology source from Single Symbol to Graduated
Set Value to Total (i.e. the UK population in 2021)
Set Method to Size
Click Classify → OK. Point sizes should now reflect population per postcode

title: 3  Geocoding and population
text:
3.2 Finding headcount statistics

Click Vector → Analysis Tools → Basic Statistics For Fields...
Set Input layer to the Wales_headcounts_at_postcodes_2021.gpkg layer
Set Field to calcualate statics on to Total
Click Run. Results are presented under the Log tab, and can be viewed in the Results Viewer. Double-clicking Statistics will open the results in a web browser
Consider what each value means, then discuss with your neighbour what the registered population of Wales in 2021 was (a sense check on google may help!)



What was the registered population of Wales in 2021? (Enter the number without commas)



The registered population of Wales in 2021 was 3,107,400.



Click Close
Calculate the percentage population change in Wales between 2011 and 2021. Show off by being first to tell your neighbour the result



What was the percentage change in the population of Wales between 2011 and 2021?



The percentage change in the population of Wales between 2011 and 2021 was 1%.



Right-click on the 2011 census headcount layer and click Remove Layer...







TipKeeping things tidy



It’s good practice to remove layers once you’re done with them, to avoid your project becoming too cluttered and confusing.

title: 3  Geocoding and population
text:
3.3 Selecting by location

Calculate basic statistics on a subset of data in a particular location:

Select the Swansea county polygon from Wales_Principal_Areas (forgotten how to do this? Check Section 1.5)
Click Vector → Research Tools → Select By Location...
Set Select features from as Wales_headcounts_at_postcodes_2021
Check are within
Set By comparing to the features from to Wales_Principal_Areas
Check Selected features only. This ensures only postcodes in Swansea are selected
Click Run
If done correctly, you’ll see all postcode centroids in Swansea county have been selected (highlighted yellow)

Use the Basic Statistics For Fields... tool to find the 2021 Total population of Swansea. Make sure Selected features only is checked this time



What was the total population of Swansea county in 2021? (Enter the number without commas)



The total population of Swansea county in 2021 was 238,447.



Calculate the 2021 population of Cardiff county



What was the total population of Cardiff county in 2021? (Enter the number without commas)



The total population of Cardiff county in 2021 was 362,356.



Calculate the percentage population change in Swansea county between 2011 and 2021. Show off again by beating your neighbour in finding the results



What was the percentage change in the population of Swansea county between 2011 and 2021? (Enter the number without commas)



The percentage change in the population of Swansea county between 2011 and 2021 was -0.2.

title: 3  Geocoding and population
text:
3.4 Creating a heatmap

Click Processing → Toolbox or find the the shortcut ()
Click the drop-down arrow next to Interpolation
Double-click Heatmap (Kernel Density Estimation)
Generate a raster heatmap of population density across Wales:

Set Point layer to Wales_headcounts_at_postcodes_2021
Set Radius to 500 metres
Set Pixel size X and Pixel size Y to 100
Set Weight from field to Total

Experiment with the raster layer’s symbology (see Section 2.5). It may help to hide the 2021 point layer and clear any selections from the principal areas polygons whilst you do this
Experiment with changing the Radius to see how the heatmap changes
Saved your project recently?

title: 3  Geocoding and population
text:
3.5 Geocoding new addresses






TipWhat’s geocoding?



Geocoding is the process of converting a human-readable address or place name into geographic coordinates, such as latitude and longitude. It allows a GIS to plot locations on a map. Let’s do some geocoding by plotting where your local Tesco stores are located!



Navigate to the Tesco store locator
Search for stores in the Swansea area
Open Excel
Populate a spreadsheet with the Store name and Postcode of the first seven stores from the website







Save the spreadsheet in a .csv format (UTF-8)
In QGIS, select Plugins → Manage and Install Plugins...







TipThe power of plugins



Plugins are written by QGIS developers and other independent developers who want to extend the core functionality of the software. It is this community-led innovating that makes QGIS such a powerful tool.



Search for mmqgis
Click Install Plugin







Use the MMQGIS tool to attach coordinates to postcode data:

Click MMQGIS → Geocode → Geocode CSV with Web Service
Set Input CSV File as your .csv file
Set Address as your postcode column
Set Web Service as OpenStreetMap / Nominatim
Set Output File Name to your Downloads folder
Set Not Found Output List to your Downloads folder
Click Apply
Wait until Geocoded 7 of 7 appears beneath the tool and check the postcodes appear in the correct places
Click Close













ImportantTemporary output



It’s common in QGIS to create temporary layers, check they’re displaying as intended, then save the output to somewhere more sensible. This is especially true if several steps are needed to create the intended output. Saving these temporary layers to your Downloads folder is a good idea, as you can eventually empty this folder without glogging up valuable space on your OneDrive account with junk data.

title: 3  Geocoding and population
text:
3.6 Exporting vector layers
Modify the temporary vector layer and save in a sensible location:
i. From the `Layers` panel, right-click on `temp1` and click `Export` → `Save Features As...`
ii. Set `Format` to `GeoPackage`
iii. Select a suitable location to save the geopackage 
iv. Set 'Layer name' as something sensible, e.g. the same as the file name
v. Set `CRS` to `EPSG:27700`
vi. Under `Select fields to export and their export options`, you can decide what information should appear in the attribute table. Keep things tidy by only including the store name and postcode
vii. Click `OK`






The layer should appear in the Layers panel. Open its attribute table. Does what you’ve just done make conceptual sense? If not - ask!
Remove the temp1 layer from your project

title: 3  Geocoding and population
text:
3.7 Using buffers as simple catchments

Create buffers around each postcode point to approximate walking distance from the Tescos store:

Click Vector → Geoprocessing Tools → Buffer...
Set Input layer as your Tesco stores layer (which should now have [EPSG:27700] after the layer name)
Set Distance to 500 metres
Check Dissolve result
Click Run → Close








Using Select by Location (see Section 3.3) and Basic Statistics (see Section 3.2), find the total number of people registered to postcodes within 500 m of Tesco stores
For the final challenge - find the total number of people registered in 2021 within 2 km of Swansea University Singleton Campus (SA2 8PQ) and Bay Campus (SA1 8QE). Hint: see Section 1.8



What was the total number of people registered in 2021 within 2 km of Swansea University Singleton Campus (SA2 8PQ) and Bay Campus (SA1 8QE)? (Enter the number without commas)



The total number of people registered in 2021 within 2 km of Swansea University Singleton Campus (SA2 8PQ) and Bay Campus (SA1 8QE) was 32,940.


The skills you’ve learned here are vital for the wind farm project.






NoteLearning outcomes



By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

Explore postcode-linked census data through the attribute table, examining and explaining spatial patterns of high and low population density
Visualise population density using graduated symbology and kernel density (heatmap) estimation
Geocode addresses from postcodes using a plugin and web service, and export the result as a properly projected vector layer
Calculate population statistics for defined areas and catchments — combining Select by Location, Buffer, and Basic Statistics for Fields tools
Appreciate how postcodes link human activity to physical location, and the value of tidy, well-projected data and temporary layers in a GIS workflow

title: 4  Combining vector layers
text:
4.1 Investigating your map tile
Creating spatial and thematic subsets of vector layers is essential GIS practice. It is through the manipulation and combination of spatial datasets that we generate new information - such as where to site a wind farm.
This exercise will guide you through the requirements for making Map 2

title: 4  Combining vector layers
text:
Launch QGIS and create a new project
From the UK_Boundaries folder, add the Wales_border.gpkg layer to your project
From the Wales_map_tiles folder, add your assigned OS map tile to your project. This layer is where your wind farm project will focus

title: 4  Combining vector layers
text:
4.2 Map tiles
Your assigned map tiles can be found here.

title: 4  Combining vector layers
text:
4.3 Clip

Add all the layers in the Wales_protected_areas folder to your project
Explore these layers and their attributes. Is it obvious what is meant by ‘protected areas’? Find more information about these datasets here.
Save your project!
Clip each protected area layer so they appear within your map tile:

Click Vector → Geoprocessing Tools → Clip...
Set Input layer to one of the protected areas layers - let’s start with NRW_AONB
Set Overlay layer to your map tile
Click Run → Close








WarningTemporary scratch layers



You’ll now see a new layer called Clipped with a memory chip icon () next to it. This means the layer is temporary. If you close QGIS now, you will lose this layer! So, shall we make it permanent? Well, we want to clip all the protected areas layers to the map tile, then combine into a single ‘protected areas’ layer (see steps below). So it’s fine to amass these temporary layers to get to the final desired layer, then remove them all without saving ‘junk’ data. This came up in the last exercise (see ?sec-tempout).



Rename the Clipped layer to something more intuitive (e.g. NRW_AONB_Clipped). It is important to rename temporary layers as you go, otherwise you’ll inevitably get confused over which layers represent what
Clip the remaining protected area datasets to your map tile. You only need to clip those layers that actually have features in your area, so inspect the layers first to find out if this is the case


4.3.1 Merge

Merge the clipped layer to create a single ‘protected area’ layer:

Click Vector → Data Management Tools → Merge Vector Layers...
Under Input layers, click the Browse icon () and check all the clipped layers
Click OK
Set Destination CRS to EPSG27700
Click Run → Close

title: 4  Combining vector layers
text:
4.4 The Dissolve tool
Combining polygons often leaves behind boundaries within the output which no longer represent the new polygon edge. These may even complicate further processing steps. It is good practice to remove these internal boundaries using the Dissolve tool.

title: 4  Combining vector layers
text:
4.5 Being efficient
Why not merge everything first, then clip and dissolve? Whilst that’s easier for us, it’s harder for the PC to merge multiple large-scale datasets. Clipping each layer individually then merging is actually more efficient for the PC. This means runtimes are faster.

title: 4  Combining vector layers
text:
4.6 Efficient filing
This is a good time to remind you to be careful and tidy about where to save GIS output – you will be generating many files for this project and a hierarchical folder structure and carefully named layers is highly recommended. Be methodical in how you name layers and where you put them – you will need to find and use them later on.

title: 4  Combining vector layers
section: 4.7 Clipping line layers and adding buffers
text:
4.7 Clipping line layers and adding buffers

From the British_Isles_geofabrik/wales folder, add the gis_osm_waterways_free_1.gpkg, gis_osm_water_a_free_1.gpkg, gis_osm_railways_free_1.gpkg, and gis_osm_roads_free_1.gpkg layers to your project
Explore these layers’ attributes
Clip each of these layers to your tile. This time, try saving each clipped layer directly to your OneDrive account. It is up to you whether you prefer saving output directly, or if you’d rather create temporary layers to inspect before making them permanet.







Review the Windfarm Project instructions and ?sec-constraints and begin to:

?sec-addlayers all the necessary layers to your project
Use ?sec-buffer to find which parts of your map tile should not be built upon
?sec-clip, Section 4.3.1, and Section 4.4.1 any orginial or modified layer as required
?sec-save your layers in sensible, well-organised file structure


Think carefully about the order in which you buffer, clip, dissolve, merge etc. Would clipping at the end of your workflow remove trailing bits generated by your buffer, for example (:egg:)? Experimentation is encouraged! You will find efficient and inefficient ways of doing things, and your learning really develops when you play around, mess up, and try again.

title: 4  Combining vector layers
text:
4.8 Selecting elements by attribute

From the British_Isles_geofabrik/wales folder, add the gis_osm_landuse_a_free_1.gpkg layer to your project
Clip the layer to your map tile
Open the layer’s attribute table
Click Select features using an expression ()
Expand Fields and Values
Click fclass → All Unique. All unique categories in the fclass layer (i.e. all the unique land use classes) are now listed
Decide which classes are relevant (again, refer to ?sec-constraits)
Under Expression, type "fclass" = 'residential'. You can also double-click on the fields, values, and symbols (e.g. ) names to build the expression
Click OK

title: 4  Combining vector layers
text:
5.1 Taking stock of planning constraints

By this point you should have a set of data layers which together represent those parts of your map tile unsuitable for windfarm development because of their position within, or proximity to, man-made or natural features of the landscape. Consider how best to present these on a map as part of your Project. Remember to think about the purpose and audience, and the need to justify your thinking







TipLearning outcomes



By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

Use the field calculator to derive geometric attributes (area, perimeter) and compute values such as population density for a map tile.
Clip features from large vector datasets to a defined area of interest, retaining only the data relevant to the analysis.
Combine multiple clipped layers into a single dataset by merging and dissolving internal boundaries to produce clean output.
Create dissolved buffers around line and polygon features to represent zones of constraint or proximity.
Select features by attribute using expressions, and organise the resulting layers methodically within a well-structured file system.

title: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed
text:
5.1 Adding rasters
Elevation is a key determinant of many geographical processes. The height of the land determines whether the coast is above or below sea level. Mountain and valley slopes determine water flow and microclimates. Biomes are often restricted to particular altitudes. Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) describe land surface height in a grid, and are a special case of continuous geospatial data widely available as raster datasets at various spatial resolutions. QGIS has several tools to inspect and manipulate DEMs, which are necessary for the wind farm project.
This exercise will guide you through the requirements for making Map 3
crumbs: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed

title: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed
text:
Launch QGIS and create a new project
From the Wales_DEM folder, add the SRTM_Wales_DEM_25m.tif layer to your project. This DEM is derived from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission, which scanned nearly 80% of Earth’s land surfaces in 2000 to generate a DEM at 25 m resolution.
From the layer’s symbology (Properties... → Symbology), experiment with the Singleband pseudocolor render type (see Section 2.5)
Click the drop-down arrow to the right of the Color ramp
Click Create New Color Ramp







Under Please select color ramp type:, select Catalog: cpt‑city. This ‘city’ of Colour Palette Tables (CPTs) is a repository of colour tables designed to creatively present raster data
Explore the Topography theme
Experiment with adjusting:

The Color ramp
Min / max under the Min / Max Value Settings drop-down menu iii.Mode (Continuous, Equal Interval, and Quantile)

Click OK
crumbs: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed

title: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed
text:
5.2 Inspecting rasters

Install the Value Tool
Click the Value Tool icon (). This tool allows you to interrogate data values as you pass the cursor over rasters
Find the heights of Yr Wyddfa (Eryri) and Pen y Fan (Bannau Brycheiniog). Check your heights against those on Google
Add the Wales_operational_windfarms.gpkg layer to your project
Reflect on where these wind farms are located. How do their locations correlate with elevation?
crumbs: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed

title: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed
text:
5.3 Clipping rasters

Clip the DEM to your map tile:

Click Raster → Extraction → Clip Raster by Mask Layer...
Set Input layer to SRTM_Wales_DEM_25m
SetMask layer to your map tile. You can access layers even if they aren’t loaded in your project using the Browse icon ()
Click the Browse icon () next to Clipped (mask) and enter a sensible file name (e.g. SH22_DEM) and location on your OneDrive account to save the clipped raster
Click Save → Run → Close
Have you saved your project recently?

Explore your map tile’s DEM using a suitable colour palette and different Min / max ranges
Identify the highest point in your clipped DEM and, if possible, its name by Googling
Here’s an opportunity to keep your project clutter-free. Remove the SRTM_Wales_DEM_25m and Wales_operational_windfarms layers from your project
crumbs: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed

title: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed
text:
5.4 Viewing maps in 3D

View the clipped DEM in 3D:

Click View → 3D Map Views → New 3D Map View
Click the Configure... icon ()
Click Terrain
Set Type to DEM (Raster Layer)
Set Elevation to your clipped DEM
Set Vertical scale to 4
Set Tile resolution to 64 px
Click OK
Use the mouse (by scrolling and holding down the click on the scroller) to explore the 3D map
Experiment with different values of Vertical scale and Tile resolution
Add other layers to see them plotted in 3D








5.4.1 Deriving a slope raster
Slope (gradient of the land surface) is fundamental properties of the land surface topography and can enlighten many geophysical processes such erosion.

Derive a slope raster from a DEM:

Click Raster → Analysis → Slope...
Set Input layer as your clipped DEM
Click the Browse icon () next to Slope to save the slope raster somewhere sensible
Click Save → Run → Close
Use the layer’s legend to identify the steepest areas. Why are they there?
crumbs: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed

title: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed
text:
5.5 Deriving an aspect raster
Aspect (compass direction towards which the gradient faces) is fundamental properties of the land surface topography and can enlighten many geophysical processes such as insolation.

Derive an aspect raster from a DEM:

Click Raster → Analysis → Aspect...
Set Input layer as your clipped DEM
Click the Browse icon () next to Aspect to save the aspect raster somewhere sensible
Click Save → Run → Close An aspect of 1° (just East of North) is very close in meaning to an aspect of 359° (just West of North), yet they are at the opposite ends of the decimal geographic coordinate numerical range. A colour palette table with the same colour for both ends of the value range would make it easier to interpret your aspect layer
Navigate to the cpt‑city colour Palette Tables (CPTs) (see Section 5.1)
Click the All by author tab
In the Name window, click grass
In the GRASS colour ramps window, click aspect Click OK → OK
crumbs: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed

title: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed
text:
5.6 Deriving a hillshade raster
Hill-shading simulates the effect of light falling on a surface by combining slope, aspect and a solar illumination direction. This approach is commonly used to visualize topography in maps and figures.

Derive a hillshade raster from a DEM:

Click Raster → Analysis → Hillshade...
Set Input layer as your clipped DEM
Click the Browse icon () next to Hillshade to save the aspect raster somewhere sensible
Click Save → Run → Close
From the Layers panel, turn off layer visibilities or arrange layers so that your hillshade layer is above your DEM layer
Change the hillshade transparency to 50%
Change the symology of your DEM to something intuitive for land height (e.g. Greens)

Experiment with Z factor (probably no more than 5) Experiment with Azimuth of the light Experiment with Altitude of the light







This is a rare example where making a layer semi-transparent can be useful. The effect is often used to make maps visually engaging
crumbs: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed

title: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed
text:
5.7 Classifying raster data
Use the raster calculator to perform cell-by-cell operations, such as to find parts of a raster layer within a specified range of values. One of the constraints for building a windfarm is that the land surface slope should be no more than 6 degrees. This is simply because greater slopes are less stable and not normally viable to build on. Build an expression in the raster calculator as follows:
i. Click `Raster` → `Raster Calculator...` 
ii. Under `Raster Bands`, double-click on the slope raster name you created earlier
iii. In the `Raster Calculation Expression` window, add `<6`
iv. Click the `Browse` icon (![](figs/Browse.png){width=3%}) next to `Output layer` to save the classified slope raster somewhere sensible
v. Click `OK`

The output raster has two values; `0` (black) and `1` (white). Given you instructed the raster calculator to identify areas of the raster that are less than 6°, what do you think these colours represent? If one can build on a slope only on land less than 6°, which colour represents suitable areas to bulid wind farms?
crumbs: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed

title: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed
text:
5.8 Converting to vector polygons
Vector polygons can be created from raster layers so that they can be combined with other vector constraints such as those created in chapter 4.

5.8.0.1 Polygonize

Convert raster classifications to vector polygons:

Click Raster → Conversion → Polygonize (Raster to Vector)...
Set Input layer as your classified slope layer
Set Name of the field to create as Suitable
Click Run → Close

Polygons now demarcate the areas that are suitable (slope < 6°) or unsuitable (slope > 6°) for building upon. Open the attribute table to explore which is which. Think binary; under the ‘Suitable’ column, 1s represent ‘yes’, 0s represent ‘no’
Visualise the suitable and unsuitable areas for construction in the symbology (see ?sec-catvec)
Select the ‘unsuitable’ polygons (Suitable = 0) using Select features using an expression (see Section 4.8)
Export the selected polygons (remember to use the Save Selected Features As... option). Name and store sensibly
crumbs: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed

title: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed
text:
5.9 Wind speeds

From the Wales_mean_windspeed folder, add the Wales_wind-speed_50m.tif layer to your project
Read over the description_and_data_source.txt file in the Wales_mean_windspeed folder for details about the data. Note; description_and_data_source.txt files appear with every dataset you use
Clip the wind speed raster to your tile and save it somewhere sensible (see Section 5.3)
Visualise the data using a suitable colour palette
crumbs: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed

title: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed
text:
5.10 Putting it all together

Reopen your constraint layers project from Exercise 4, and add your polygonised slope constraint
With the wind speed layer beneath constraints, explore where development may be permitted and optimal. you can explore not just where building a windfarm may be permitted, but where the windiest (best power generation) and largest (most number of turbines possible) plots of land are located in your map tile area
Design Map 3 of your wind farm Project to clearly show the best otherwise‑unconstrained wind farm location, and use the various tools (e.g raster calculator) to extract information to help you justify why







TipLearning outcomes



By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

Visualise raster elevation data using pseudocolour ramps, cpt-city palettes, and min/max scaling, and interrogate cell values directly with the Value Tool.
Clip raster layers to an area of interest and explore the resulting surface in three dimensions.
Derive slope, aspect, and hillshade rasters from a DEM, and explain what each reveals about surface topography and geophysical process.
Classify raster data with the raster calculator to identify areas meeting a defined threshold, and convert the result to vector polygons for combination with other constraint layers.
Appreciate how elevation, slope, and wind speed interact to determine site suitability, integrating raster-derived constraints into a justified development decision.
crumbs: 5  Elevation, slope, and wind speed

title: 6  Wind farm area polygon, viewshed, and impact
text:
6.1 Starting point
This exercise is all about applying the skills you’ve gained over the past five exercises, to cement your GIS skills and successfully complete the wind farm project. You will also create a new polygon to represent your wind farm location, and create viewsheds to identify who may be impacted by the wind farm development.
This exercise will guide you through the requirements for making Map 4

title: 6  Wind farm area polygon, viewshed, and impact
text:
6.2 Wind farm polygon creation

6.2.0.1 Create new vector layer

Create a new GeoPackage vector layer representing your optimal wind farm location:

Click Layer → Create Layer → New GeoPackage Layer...
Click the Browse icon () next to Dataset to save the wind farm location vector somewhere sensible
Set Geometry type as Polygon
Set the CRS as EPSG:27700
Click OK
From the Layers panel, right‑click on the new layer and click Toggle Editing or find the shortcut ()

You can tell when a layer’s in edit mode, as a pencil icon appears over the layer’s symbol. Edits are temporary until you save them. This allows you to undo any mistakes you may have made. But beware - once saved, mistakes can’t be undone!

From the Digitizing Toolbar, click Add Polygon Feature







Left‑click on the Map Canvas to draw vertices (points), outlining your optimum wind farm location
Once your polygon is complete, right‑click to finish
click OK
If necessary, adjust the polygon by:

Clicking the Vertex Tool ()
Selecting a polygon vertex
Moving the cursor to the desired location and pressing left-click

Click the Toggle Editing icon () once more to turn off editing
Click Save

title: 6  Wind farm area polygon, viewshed, and impact
text:
6.3 Enable snapping
Are you a perfectionist, but you can’t get the edge of your optimum wind farm area to abut a constraint layer? Well the snapping tool is for you! This will pull the cursor up against the edge of a vector layer to aid in the perfect placement of vertices. Try it out by clicking View → Toolbars → Snapping Toolbar, then clicking the Enable Snapping icon ().
crumbs: 6  Wind farm area polygon, viewshed, and impact

title: 6  Wind farm area polygon, viewshed, and impact
section: 6.4 How big is your wind farm?
text:
6.4 How big is your wind farm?

Calculate the area of the polygon (see Section 4.2.0.1)

A 50 m turbine generates about 750kWh . How many turbines will your windfarm support? Note that as long as your area is at least 150m across at its narrowest point it is big enough for at least one turbine, so is viable.

To create:

Click Vector → Research Tools → Create Grid...
Set Grid type as Hexagon (Polygon)
Under Grid extent, click the drop-down arrow → Calculate from Layer → select your wind farm location polygon
Set Horizontal spacing and Vertical spacing to 50 metres
Set Grid CRS as EPSG:27700
Click OK → Close
Click Vector → Geometry Tools → Centroids...
Set Input layer to the new Grid layer
Click Run → Close
Create buffer around those points
Use Select by Location... BUT this time, only are within for your wind farm site(see)
Export, check ‘save selected features’
Use attribute table to count number of turbines
Calculate their potential energy output in kWh
crumbs: 6  Wind farm area polygon, viewshed, and impact

title: 6  Wind farm area polygon, viewshed, and impact
text:
6.5 Creating a viewshed

Install the Visibility Analysis plugin.
Create a centroid point for your wind farm polygon (Vector → Geometry Tools → Centroids). This point represents the wind farm location for viewshed analysis.
In the Processing Toolbox, run Visibility Analysis → Create Viewpoints. Set Observer locations = wind farm centroid; DEM = your tile DEM; Radius of analysis = 10 km; Observer height = 50 m; Target height = 2 m. Save the output viewpoint layer.
Run Visibility Analysis → Analysis → Viewshed using the viewpoint layer and your tile DEM. Explore and understand the result.
crumbs: 6  Wind farm area polygon, viewshed, and impact

title: 6  Wind farm area polygon, viewshed, and impact
text:
6.6 Calculating impact

Vectorise your viewshed (see Exercise 05) to create polygons representing areas within 10 km from which the wind farm is visible. Use select‑by‑value and save selected features.
Using methods from Exercise 03, calculate the total number of people registered at postcodes within line‑of‑sight. If errors about “invalid geometry” occur, buffer the visibility polygon by 1 m and retry.
Design Map 4 to present the wind farm location/extent and its visual impact. Focus on population and visibility; you do not need to repeat earlier context maps.
Comment in your CW4 caption on how well your analysis captures potential impact if your wind farm lies near the tile edge.







TipLearning outcomes



By the end of this exercise you should:

Create and edit a vector layer in QGIS.
Create a new polygon layer to represent a proposed wind farm location.
Calculate the area of a vector polygon and estimate turbine capacity.
Create a viewshed using an observer/target and a DEM.
Quantify population within sight of the proposed wind farm and its proportion of the tile population.
